newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin vows to minimise security threat from NATO.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin vows to minimise security threat from NATO.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin has said he will do all he can to minimise any threat posed to Russia by NATO's eastward expansion.

"We will do everything to minimise the consequences of possible NATO enlargement for Russia's security," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying in an interview to be published on Wednesday by the defence ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvevda.
Yeltsin gave no details but said he would press on with efforts to deepen integration between Russia and other former Soviet republics and to develop ties with China.
Moscow opposes NATO's plans to offer membership to former members of the Soviet bloc, saying such enlargement threatens Russia's security.
But Yeltsin hopes to sign an agreement with NATO on May 27 setting out terms for a peaceful new relationship with the Western defence alliance, Moscow's former Cold War enemy.
Western diplomats say Russia has been trying to win as many concessions as possible to ease the pain of NATO expansion.

Yeltsin said in the interview, marking five years since the creation of the Russian armed forces following the collapse of the Soviet Union, that he would push on with plans to create a completely professional, non-conscript army.
"No matter how unrealistic this might seem because of current financial shortages, we must have such a goal and strive for its achievement," he said.

Yeltsin has announced plans to cut down the size of the armed forces under reforms which have made little progress. The concept for change has not been finalised and there are differences over how to carry them out.
"Reductions of the armed forces must not be mechanical or reckless. A lessening of the troops' strength must be compensated with better equipment, training and skills," he said.
Yeltsin also said he was determined to root out corruption in the armed forces. Several senior officers have been dismissed and face corruption charges under this campaign.
"The pest of corruption, bribe-taking and theft has unfortunately affected the armed forces and many other state institutions. We need to resolutely do away with this dirt," he said.
